messages.content: What are the different properties of Hydrogen?

message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe – has a range of distinctive physical, chemical, and nuclear properties:

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Standard atomic weight** | ~1.008 u (average of isotopes) |
| **Isotopes** | ¹H (protium, 99.98 %), ²H (deuterium, 0.02 %) and trace amounts of ³H (tritium, radioactive). |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative, meaning energy is released when an electron is added) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) at 1 atm |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) at 1 atm |
| **Density** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (very low; lighter than air) |
| **Molar volume** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ at STP |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas |
| **Solubility in water** | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ (soluble but limited) |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, reacts with halogens, oxygen, and many other elements. |
| **Bonding** | Forms covalent bonds (single H–H bond), ionic bonds (as H⁺ or H⁻), and participates in hydrogen bonding (in water, alcohols, etc.). |
| **Acidity/Basicity** | In aqueous solution, behaves as a weak acid (hydronium formation). As a base, it can accept a proton to form H₂O. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) – classic hydrogen emission spectrum. |
| **Nuclear properties** | Proton (¹H) is stable; deuterium is stable; tritium decays via β⁻ decay (half‑life ≈12.32 y). |
| **Applications** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen), laboratory reagent, metal hydride storage, spectroscopy standard. |

These values illustrate why hydrogen is unique: its single proton and electron make it the lightest element, while its ability to form both covalent and ionic bonds gives it versatility across chemistry, physics, and engineering.
